title: Super Mario Odyssey Review: Nintendo’s 3D Platforming Playground
description: Super Mario Odyssey turns movement, possession, and discovery into a joyful globe-trotting platformer packed with playful ideas.
body:
Super Mario Odyssey arrives with the confidence of a series that has spent decades redefining how movement can feel. Mario's basic controls are already excellent, but Cappy transforms familiar platforming into something more flexible: a traversal tool, a weapon, a temporary platform, and a way to possess dozens of creatures and objects across the world.

The result is one of Nintendo's most generous 3D platformers. Kingdoms constantly introduce new mechanics, Power Moons reward almost every kind of curiosity, and Mario's moveset gives skilled players enormous freedom to improvise routes that beginners may never realize are possible.

That abundance occasionally works against the game. Some Moons are so easy or repetitive that individual discoveries can feel less special, and a handful of captures exist more as amusing ideas than fully developed mechanics. Even so, Odyssey's best moments are Nintendo design at its most playful: movement feels wonderful, surprises arrive constantly, and almost every kingdom contains something worth poking, climbing, throwing Cappy at, or trying to reach the wrong way.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: Mario poses beside Cappy against a red world-map background in official promotional artwork for Super Mario Odyssey.
imageCredit: Nintendo / Super Mario Odyssey official promotional artwork.

cons: The huge number of Power Moons makes many individual rewards feel less meaningful
Some captures are clever one-off ideas rather than deep mechanics
Motion-control shortcuts are less comfortable for players who prefer standard inputs
A portion of the late-game Moon hunting leans on repetition and filler
pros: Mario has one of the most expressive and satisfying movesets in the series
Cappy and captures constantly reinvent how levels can be explored
Kingdoms are packed with visual variety and playful ideas
Power Moons reward experimentation and curiosity at almost every turn
Excellent presentation, music, animation, and post-game content
reviewMeta.verdict: A joyful, inventive 3D platformer with extraordinary movement and constant surprises, held back only slightly by an overabundance of low-impact collectibles and a few underdeveloped ideas.

contentBlocks.text:
Odyssey begins with one of the strongest foundations in 3D platforming: Mario himself. Running, long jumping, rolling, wall jumping, ground pounding, diving, and chaining those moves together feels precise without becoming inaccessible.

Cappy pushes that movement even further. Throwing the hat can extend jumps, alter momentum, activate objects, and create temporary footholds. Skilled players can combine cap throws and dives to reach places that look impossible, while newcomers can still finish the game using a much simpler set of moves.

That layered design is one of Odyssey's greatest strengths. The game rarely demands advanced technique, but it constantly rewards players who want to learn it. Movement becomes a form of expression rather than merely transportation between objectives.
contentBlocks.heading: Mario Has Never Felt Better to Control

contentBlocks.text:
The capture mechanic allows Mario to temporarily control enemies, creatures, and objects, giving each kingdom a different set of verbs. A Goomba can stack with others, a Bullet Bill can cross long gaps, a Pokio can climb walls with its beak, and a Tropical Wiggler can stretch across spaces Mario cannot.

The best captures feel like compact platforming systems. Nintendo introduces a rule, builds several challenges around it, then moves on before the idea loses its novelty. That rhythm keeps the game fresh because Mario is constantly learning a new relationship with the environment.

Not every capture is equally deep. Some exist primarily for a joke, a single puzzle, or a brief visual surprise. But even the shallow ones contribute to the sense that nearly anything in Odyssey might become interactive once Cappy is involved.
contentBlocks.heading: Cappy Turns Every Kingdom Into a Toy Box

contentBlocks.text:
Odyssey's kingdoms are not enormous open worlds. They are dense playgrounds built around recognizable landmarks, hidden routes, layered vertical spaces, and enough secrets to make revisiting them worthwhile.

That scale works beautifully. Players can develop a mental map of each kingdom while still discovering alcoves, challenges, characters, doors, and Power Moons long after the main objective is complete. Sand Kingdom feels fundamentally different from Metro Kingdom, which feels different from Luncheon Kingdom, yet all of them are designed around Mario's mobility.

The strongest spaces encourage playful rule-breaking. A visible rooftop or distant ledge becomes a challenge even when the game never explicitly asks the player to reach it. Often, Nintendo has hidden something there anyway.
contentBlocks.heading: The Kingdoms Are Small Enough to Learn and Dense Enough to Surprise

contentBlocks.text:
Power Moons are everywhere. They can be earned through platforming challenges, races, puzzles, exploration, NPC interactions, hidden rooms, minigames, clever captures, or simply noticing something suspicious in the environment.

This abundance makes Odyssey extremely welcoming. Progress rarely depends on solving one specific challenge, so players can follow whatever interests them and still keep moving. The game constantly says yes to curiosity.

The downside is that not every Moon feels important. Some are earned through memorable challenges; others are sitting behind a corner, under a glowing patch of ground, or attached to a very simple interaction. When rewards are this common, the emotional difference between an ingenious discovery and an effortless pickup becomes smaller than it should be.
contentBlocks.heading: Power Moons Make Curiosity Almost Always Worthwhile

contentBlocks.text:
Metro Kingdom is the clearest demonstration of Odyssey's identity. New Donk City combines vertical exploration, movement challenges, characters, secrets, music, and a playful collision between Mario's cartoon logic and a more urban setting.

The kingdom is immediately readable but full of routes. Fire escapes, rooftops, poles, taxis, power lines, and interior challenges turn the city into a platforming space without making it feel like a traditional obstacle course.

Odyssey repeatedly reaches this level of confidence when a kingdom's theme, captures, movement, and presentation all reinforce one another. These are the moments when it feels less like a collection hunt and more like Nintendo discovering another way to make moving through a 3D space delightful.
contentBlocks.heading: New Donk City Captures Odyssey at Its Best

contentBlocks.text:
Super Mario Odyssey is colorful without becoming visually noisy. Each kingdom has a strong identity, character animation is expressive, and small reactions give both Mario and Cappy enormous personality.

The soundtrack moves comfortably between orchestral adventure, playful regional themes, and vocal set pieces that give major moments a sense of occasion. Nintendo understands exactly when to let nostalgia surface and when to push Mario into something stranger.

The game also treats its own history with warmth rather than reverence. Costumes, 2D sections, references, familiar enemies, and musical callbacks appear throughout the journey, but Odyssey rarely feels trapped by them. It uses Mario's past as another toy rather than a set of rules it must obey.
contentBlocks.heading: Presentation Makes the Adventure Feel Like a Celebration

contentBlocks.text:
Finishing the main story opens a much larger layer of challenges, additional objectives, and reasons to return to earlier kingdoms. For players who love Mario's movement, this is where some of the game's most demanding platforming appears.

It is also where Odyssey's collectible philosophy becomes most uneven. The enormous Moon count gives completionists a long runway, but some objectives are repeated, trivial, or dependent on activities that are more time-consuming than interesting.

The strongest post-game Moons test mastery of movement or ask the player to reinterpret familiar spaces. The weakest feel like numbers added to extend the checklist. Odyssey contains so many great ideas that the filler is easy to forgive, but it still prevents the reward structure from feeling as consistently sharp as the movement itself.
contentBlocks.heading: The Post-Game Is Huge, but Not Every Moon Earns Its Place

contentBlocks.text:
Odyssey rarely tells players there is only one correct way to move through a space. A beginner can follow the obvious path, while an experienced player may chain jumps, cap throws, dives, and captures into a completely different route.

That freedom is the reason the game remains compelling after the story ends. Even when individual Power Moons lose some of their value through overabundance, Mario himself never becomes less enjoyable to control.

Nintendo's best 3D platformers understand that movement should be fun before the reward at the end of the movement is even considered. Super Mario Odyssey follows that principle almost perfectly.
contentBlocks.heading: A Platformer Built Around Joyful Possibility

conclusion:
==Super Mario Odyssey is one of Nintendo's most confident 3D platformers, combining an exceptionally expressive moveset with kingdoms that constantly reward curiosity. Cappy and the capture system give the game a steady stream of mechanical surprises, while Mario's movement is deep enough to make simply crossing a level enjoyable.==

==The huge Power Moon count occasionally weakens the sense of achievement, and not every capture or late-game challenge is developed equally. Those are small imperfections inside an adventure overflowing with creativity. Odyssey succeeds because its greatest reward is not the collectible at the end of a challenge; it is the joy of figuring out how Mario can get there.==
